summary: MLD is used by an IPv6 router to learn which multicast addresses its neighbors want. MLDv2 adds source filtering, so a node can state interest in traffic only from specific sources, and it is designed to work alongside MLDv1. This internet-standard text obsoletes RFC 3810.

plainLanguage.summary: Multicast Listener Discovery tells an IPv6 router which multicast groups have listeners on its local links. MLDv2 also lets a listener name sources it wants or sources it excludes, so routers can limit multicast forwarding accordingly.

subtitle: How IPv6 routers learn which multicast groups and sources their neighboring nodes want.

tldr.problem: An IPv6 multicast router needs to know which multicast addresses and source addresses have interested listeners on each directly attached link.
tldr.mechanism: A Querier sends MLD Queries, and nodes report current listening state or changes using INCLUDE or EXCLUDE filters and source lists. Routers combine that information and use timers and follow-up queries before pruning traffic.
tldr.outcome: MLDv2 supports source filtering and is designed to interoperate with MLDv1. RFC 9777 is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 3810 and updates RFC 2710.

today: RFC 9777 is an Internet Standard published in March 2025. It obsoletes RFC 3810 and updates RFC 2710.

sections.title: What MLDv2 Does
sections.content:
Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) lets IPv6 routers learn which neighboring nodes want multicast traffic on a directly attached link. MLDv2 adds source filtering: a node can request traffic for a multicast address only from selected sources, or from every source except selected ones. This supports Source-Specific Multicast and is designed to interoperate with MLDv1.

MLD has separate listener and router behavior. The router maintains link-level information and passes it to its multicast routing protocol. It need only know that at least one node on the link wants traffic for a given group and source; it does not have to track every listener individually.
sections.plainLanguage: MLD tells IPv6 routers which groups and senders have listeners on each link. MLDv2 adds a way to request or exclude particular sources.

sections.title: Listener State and Source Filters
sections.content:
An application asks its IP layer to listen for a multicast address using a filter mode and a source list. INCLUDE means receive only from listed sources. EXCLUDE means receive from all sources except those listed. A later request for the same socket, interface and group replaces the earlier request.

A node keeps per-socket state and derives one record per multicast address for each interface. When all sockets use INCLUDE, the interface source list is their union. If any socket uses EXCLUDE, the interface uses EXCLUDE and combines the lists to satisfy all sockets. Routers keep per-link state with a filter mode and timers for the group and its sources.
sections.plainLanguage: INCLUDE names sources to receive; EXCLUDE names sources to block. A node combines the requests from its applications into one listening state for each group on each interface.

sections.title: Queries and Reports
sections.content:
MLDv2 messages are ICMPv6 messages. They use a link-local source address, Hop Limit 1 and a Router Alert option. The checksum covers the whole message and an IPv6 pseudo-header and must be verified before processing.

Query messages use ICMPv6 Type 130. A General Query asks which groups have listeners; a Multicast Address Specific Query asks about one group; a Multicast Address and Source Specific Query asks about selected sources in a group. General Queries are sent to ff02::1, while the specific queries go to the multicast address being checked.

Version 2 Reports use Type 143 and are sent to ff02::16. A report contains one or more Multicast Address Records with a record type, group address and source list. Current-State records answer a Query; State-Change records announce a change in a listener's filter mode or source list.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers ask Queries about groups or sources, and nodes answer with Reports. A report records whether a node wants only listed sources or wants all sources except those listed.

sections.title: Listener Reports and Query Responses
sections.content:
When a listener's per-interface state changes, it sends a State-Change Report immediately. The record identifies a filter-mode change or sources newly allowed or blocked. To tolerate packet loss, state-change reports are retransmitted according to the Robustness Variable. Periodic Queries receive delayed Current-State Reports so many listeners do not reply at once.

When a listener receives a valid Query, it chooses a random response delay up to the Maximum Response Delay. It can combine pending responses for the same group. A General Query response reports each group with listening state; a source-specific response reports only sources that match the query and the listener's filter.
sections.plainLanguage: A listener reports changes promptly and repeats those reports to reduce the effect of packet loss. It delays answers to Queries by a random amount so replies are spread across the response period.

sections.title: Router State, Querier and Fast Leave
sections.content:
Only one router per link is in Querier state and sends Queries. Other routers listen and maintain the same state so one can take over if the Querier disappears. Routers elect the Querier using IPv6 link-local addresses; a router that hears a Query from a lower address becomes a Non-Querier.

Routers track group and source timers. If a listener stops requesting a group or source, the Querier sends a specific Query to check whether another listener remains. If no listener reports interest before the relevant timer expires, the router removes that state and can stop forwarding that traffic to the link. This is the fast-leave process.

The Robustness Variable defaults to 2 and can be increased for expected packet loss. The Query Interval defaults to 125 seconds, and the Query Response Interval defaults to 10000 milliseconds.
sections.plainLanguage: One router asks the periodic questions, while the others keep matching state. Before stopping traffic after a listener leaves, the Querier checks whether another listener still wants it.

sections.title: Interoperation with MLDv1
sections.content:
MLDv2 distinguishes MLDv1 Queries by their length: an MLDv1 Query is 24 octets, while an MLDv2 Query is at least 28 octets. Hosts and routers track compatibility state and temporarily use MLDv1 behavior when they detect an older-version router or listener.

With an MLDv1 router on the link, the Querier must use the lowest MLD version present, with the mode ensured through configuration. Routers translate MLDv1 Report and Done messages into corresponding MLDv2 state changes. Operators can disable compatibility behavior where source filtering is critical, but then older nodes cannot interoperate normally.
sections.plainLanguage: MLDv2 hosts and routers can switch to MLDv1 behavior when older devices are present. Administrators can disable that fallback when a network needs source filtering more than backward compatibility.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
MLD provides no cryptographic authentication, confidentiality or replay protection. Replayed messages can keep forwarding state active longer than needed, and on-link observers can learn which multicast groups nodes request.

Before acting on a message, nodes check the source address, Hop Limit and Router Alert option to reject messages that appear to come from off-link. These checks do not stop an attacker on the same link. A forged Query can claim the Querier role, and forged MLDv1 messages can trigger compatibility behavior. Implementations may limit the number of sources recorded from source-specific Queries to reduce resource-exhaustion risk.
sections.plainLanguage: MLD messages are not signed or private, so a device on the same link can forge them or inspect group interests. Address and Hop Limit checks help reject messages that come from outside the link.
